probes.query: One column of my model is filled in by the database engine itself at the moment a row is first stored; my code never supplies a value for it. After I save the new object, the Python attribute shows the stored value. Describe how that value reaches the object, and why the route differs between PostgreSQL and MySQL.
expectedFacts: BaseExecutor.execute_insert (base/executor.py:328) takes a dynamic INSERT path when an instance still holds the database-default placeholder (_has_db_default_values :224, _execute_insert_dynamic :312).
_build_insert_with_defaults (base/executor.py:234) leaves placeholder columns out of the INSERT and calls the _add_returning_to_insert hook, which does nothing in the base class (:299).
CRITICAL: On PostgreSQL the hook adds RETURNING for those columns (base_postgres/executor.py:107) and _process_insert_result (:118) sets the returned values on the instance.

CRITICAL: On MySQL there is no RETURNING; _process_insert_result (mysql/executor.py:150-159) calls _fetch_db_defaults_after_insert (base/executor.py:363), which SELECTs the columns by primary key and sets them on the instance.
The follow-up SELECT is skipped when Meta.fetch_db_defaults is false, when the model has no database-default columns, or when the pk is None (base/executor.py:370-392).
probes.author: r3h-tortoise-orm-drafter
probes.notes: CHEAPEST ROUTE: (1) grep the question words (none hit); open Model.save in models.py (grep 'def save' hits models.py + 7 client files); (2) follow save -> executor.execute_insert in backends/base/executor.py; (3) read execute_insert / _build_insert_with_defaults and find the _add_returning_to_insert hook; (4) open base_postgres/executor.py for the RETURNING override and its _process_insert_result; (5) open mysql/executor.py and find _fetch_db_defaults_after_insert back in the base executor. 5 dependent steps. FIRST GREPS: 'stored value' -> no files; 'filled in' -> no files; 'after save|def save' -> models.py and client files only (no gold file; models.py is not gold). Agent-knowledge guesses 'db_default'/'RETURNING' would reach gold but are not question words. DECOYS: bulk path BulkCreateQuery._analyze_db_default_fields (queryset.py:2163, r3-22), pk read-back (_process_insert_result for generated pk, r3-08). VERIFICATION: read base/executor.py:224-408, base_postgres/executor.py:96-131, mysql/executor.py:150-162, sqlite/executor.py:32-82 (SQLite uses RETURNING too; acceptable extra), odbc/executor.py:7-16. Closed-book risk: low (generic ORM knowledge does not give the hook names). est. turns: 7.

probes.query: A migration fails halfway through its stages. What decides whether the schema changes already made by earlier stages of that same migration are undone? List every piece of code that takes part in that decision, including the one that makes the answer depend on the database engine.
expectedFacts: Migration.atomic is a class attribute defaulting to True (migrations/migration.py:15), and MigrationExecutor.migrate builds the schema editor with atomic=migration.atomic (migrations/executor.py:86, :107).
CRITICAL: BaseSchemaEditor.__init__ sets atomic_migration = connection.capabilities.can_rollback_ddl and atomic (migrations/schema_editor/base.py:62).

When atomic_migration is true, migrate wraps the whole apply or unapply in in_transaction and swaps schema_editor.client for the transaction client (migrations/executor.py:87-96, :108-117); recording the migration happens afterwards, outside the transaction (:119-120).

CRITICAL: can_rollback_ddl is True only for the PostgreSQL family (base_postgres/client.py:54) and SQLite (sqlite/client.py:62, :288); the Capabilities default is False (base/client.py:88), so MySQL, MSSQL and Oracle are never whole-migration atomic.

Otherwise Migration._run_database_forward and _backward give an operation its own transaction only if the editor is not atomic, not collecting SQL, the client supports_transactions, and operation.atomic or (migration.atomic and operation.atomic is not False) holds (migrations/migration.py:139-185); schema operations default to atomic=False, RunPython and RunSQL to None.

SqliteSchemaEditor._run_sql in atomic mode splits the script on ';' and runs each statement through execute_query because executescript issues an implicit COMMIT (migrations/schema_editor/sqlite.py:33-51).
